abstract: Proteins interact with a wide range of biomolecular partners, yet identifying the interaction sites that mediate these events remains a major challenge for understanding cellular function and guiding drug discovery. Existing computational methods are typically designed for specific interaction classes and often rely on task-specific features. Here, we introduce PRIME-ISP, a structure-based framework for predicting interaction sites across diverse biomolecular interaction types using a unified architecture. PRIME-ISP represents proteins at five organizational levels, including solvent-excluded surfaces, atoms, residues, secondary-structure elements, and whole proteins, and integrates information across these scales through coupled bottom-up and top-down propagation. This hierarchical representation jointly captures local geometry and global structural context, enabling a single architecture to address chemically and geometrically distinct binding problems without task-specific modifications. We evaluate PRIME-ISP on protein, peptide, DNA, RNA, small-molecule, metal, and carbohydrate interaction-site prediction benchmarks. Across these tasks, PRIME-ISP consistently outperforms a recent unified sequence-based predictor and achieves performance comparable to specialized methods while requiring no interaction-specific features. These results demonstrate that hierarchical structural representations provide a flexible foundation for interaction-site prediction across diverse biomolecular interactions. Source code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/HySonLab/PRIME-ISP
